guides.title: Getting around Budapest: a first-visit transport guide
guides.description: Understand Budapest public transport, single-ticket validation, travelcards, BudapestGO and the special ticket for the 100E Airport Express.
guides.intro: Start with the places you want to visit, then choose transport that fits your day. Walking works well for compact sightseeing stops; metro, tram and bus connections help you cover the gaps. The main thing to get right is the ticket you hold and how it must be used.
highlights: Buy through official BKK channels
Validate single tickets correctly
100E Airport Express uses a special fare

sections.title: Group your stops before choosing transport
paragraphs: Put nearby sights together: one outing for Castle Hill, another for downtown Pest and a separate block for City Park. This avoids turning each attraction into a cross-city journey. Start and finish with the address of your accommodation, not just the neighbourhood name.

For your first day, keep one simple route saved and leave time to find the stop or platform. Use BKK’s current journey information when you travel; this guide does not provide live routing or disruption notices.

sections.title: Buying a single ticket is not the last step
paragraphs: BKK explains that single tickets need validation when you start travelling. Paper tickets use a validator; digital tickets follow the scanning instructions in BudapestGO. Keep the validated ticket available throughout the journey.

A regular single ticket generally covers one uninterrupted ride, with a metro-transfer exception when continuing in the same direction. For a journey involving other transfers, compare time-based tickets or a travelcard instead of assuming one single ticket covers everything.

sections.title: Single tickets, timed tickets or a travelcard?
paragraphs: Think about your actual pattern: two journeys surrounding a long walking day are different from repeatedly crossing between districts. Check the products currently offered by BKK, then compare the options for your intended journeys.

BKK’s 30- and 90-minute digital tickets allow transfers within their rules, but require scanning when you change vehicles. Daily travelcards allow unlimited transfers within their validity and do not require single-ticket-style validation. Read the current product conditions before buying.

sections.title: Airport journeys: check the 100E fare separately
paragraphs: The airport describes 100E Airport Express as a direct connection between Liszt Ferenc Airport and Deák Ferenc tér in central Pest. It requires a special ticket, so do not assume your regular city single ticket covers the airport journey.

Choose a route from the airport to your actual accommodation and reverse that check before departure. Allow for luggage, walking to your stop and check-in requirements. Current airport stopping patterns and timetables should come from the operator, not a fixed travel-time promise in a guide.

sections.title: Small habits that make the day easier
paragraphs: Save your hotel address and an offline note of the route back. Keep your phone charged if your ticket is digital, and check what you must show during inspection. For accessibility needs, examine the specific service and stop rather than assuming every connection is step-free.

Use official BKK sales channels and check the fare there before purchasing. As an editorial suggestion, leave a little flexibility in your first journey instead of booking a timed attraction immediately after arrival.
bullets: Check your route shortly before leaving.
Read ticket conditions before payment.
Keep tickets and booking confirmations within easy reach.

faqs.question: Can I use a regular single ticket on the 100E?
faqs.answer: No. BKK states that regular single tickets are not valid on 100E Airport Express. Check the current airport-ticket options directly with BKK.

faqs.question: Do daily travelcards need single-ticket validation?
faqs.answer: BKK says daily travelcards and passes do not require validation. Follow any instructions to show the ticket or pass, and use it within its validity.

guides.title: Buda Castle District: a self-guided first visit
guides.description: Plan a self-guided Castle District visit around Fisherman’s Bastion, Matthias Church, Trinity Square and time to wander.
guides.intro: The Castle District is most rewarding when you give it more than a photo stop. Start with its familiar landmarks, then leave room for the streets between them. This is a suggested walking sequence, not a timed tour: adjust the distance and number of interiors to your own pace.
highlights: Start around Trinity Square
Separate the Bastion’s lower and upper-level access
Leave space for a quieter stretch of the district

sections.title: Choose a comfortable approach
paragraphs: Castle Hill deserves a little arrival planning. Check a current BKK route from your accommodation and decide whether you want to walk up or reduce the climb. For anyone with mobility needs, review the approach and venue access independently; a viewpoint being nearby does not mean the route is step-free.

Our suggestion is to reserve a half-day if you want a mix of streets, viewpoints and an interior visit. That is an editorial allowance, not an official tour duration. If you have only a short window, focus on one part of the district rather than rushing across it.

sections.title: Begin at Trinity Square and Matthias Church
paragraphs: Use Trinity Square as an orientation point. The district’s official visitor guide groups Matthias Church, Fisherman’s Bastion and the Holy Trinity Column around this square, which makes it a useful place to start your visit.

Pause to take in the church exterior before choosing whether to go inside. Check the church’s own website for the visitor schedule and tickets on your date. Do not build a tightly timed route around opening hours copied from an old article or a search snippet.

sections.title: Fisherman’s Bastion: understand the two levels
paragraphs: Visit Budavár lists the lower level as free and the upper lookout as paid. Explore the lower terraces and take in the view across to Pest before deciding whether you want the additional upper-level access.

Give yourself time to look beyond a single photo angle. Consider a later walk along the Buda riverbank as a second perspective on the same cityscape. This is a suggestion for variety, not a promise of a particular sunset, weather or crowd level.

sections.title: Leave the main viewpoints behind for a while
paragraphs: Continue to Tóth Árpád Promenade for a change of outlook. The district visitor guide describes a walk along the castle wall with views towards the Buda hills. It offers a different direction to look after spending time facing the Danube.

Choose a manageable loop and pause before adding another major stop. If you continue towards the palace area, treat any museum interior as a separate decision with its own opening hours and tickets. You can enjoy the neighbourhood without trying to enter every building.

sections.title: Finish without rushing the descent
paragraphs: Keep the return journey flexible. You might spend more time in the district, continue towards the river or use a current public-transport connection back to Pest. Check your onward route before committing to a long downhill walk.

Wear shoes you are comfortable walking in and leave space for rests. In poor weather, shorten the outdoor route rather than trying to keep every viewpoint. A slower visit with fewer stops is still a complete Castle District experience.
bullets: Check church access on your date.
Treat each paid attraction separately.
Plan the approach and return around your mobility needs.

faqs.question: Do I need one ticket for the whole Castle District?
faqs.answer: No single ticket is required simply to explore the neighbourhood’s public streets. Individual venues and paid lookout areas have their own admission arrangements.

faqs.question: How long should I allow?
faqs.answer: Our suggested allowance is a half-day for unhurried wandering and an optional interior. Adapt that to your mobility, interests and any confirmed entry times.

guides.title: Budapest Danube cruises: daytime, evening or dinner?
guides.description: Choose a Budapest river cruise by route, daylight, departure pier and inclusions, with practical advice before you book.
guides.intro: A river cruise can be an easy way to enjoy Budapest from a new angle, but the right choice depends on what you want from the outing. Start with a simple question: are you mainly interested in the views, an evening atmosphere or a meal on board? Then compare the actual ticket details rather than the headline photograph.
highlights: Choose the experience before comparing tickets
Confirm the precise pier and boarding time
Check operational notices before departure

sections.title: Start with the format
paragraphs: For a first visit, our suggestion is to choose sightseeing if the river views are the main reason you are going. A dinner cruise makes sense when you specifically want the meal as part of the evening. Compare the total time on board, seating arrangements and what is included before deciding.

Do not compare a basic sightseeing ticket with a meal package as if they were equivalent. Think about your group, the time you have and whether commentary, music or dining is more important to you. Children, dietary needs and accessibility can change the choice.

sections.title: Daytime versus evening
paragraphs: Daylight can suit visitors who want to study the buildings and orient themselves between Buda and Pest. For an evening outing, check the actual departure time for your date rather than assuming that every evening-labelled sailing happens after dark. The season changes that calculation.

Legenda separates its daytime Duna Bella sightseeing trips from its evening Danube Legend programme. Use those operator descriptions as examples of the distinction, then read the inclusions of the exact departure you are considering.

sections.title: Do not assume an island stop is operating
paragraphs: River conditions can affect the advertised route. At the time of this guide’s check, Legenda displayed a low-water notice stating that daytime sightseeing boats could not dock at Margaret Island and were temporarily following the evening route.

That is an operational notice, not a permanent description of all Budapest cruises. Read the current provider notices before booking, especially if getting off at a particular stop is your main reason for choosing a sailing.

sections.title: Check the pier as carefully as the time
paragraphs: Use the meeting point on your booking confirmation and find it before your departure day if possible. The Danube has multiple boarding locations: a riverside neighbourhood or a recognisable landmark is not precise enough to identify your boat.

Leave time for the walk to the pier, any check-in and boarding. If you need step-free access, ask about the specific vessel and boarding arrangements before paying. Do not assume that all boats or water levels produce the same access conditions.

sections.title: What to compare before booking
paragraphs: Write down the essentials from each ticket: route, duration, commentary language, included drinks or meal, indoor seating, cancellation terms and the correct departure point. Compare the list rather than a promotional starting price.

GoToBudapest is providing a planning guide here. Live availability and booking are not connected yet, so follow the operator’s official site for current products and terms. A waterfront walk remains a good alternative if you prefer to keep the evening flexible.
bullets: Read current operational notices.
Confirm the precise meeting point.
Check cancellation and weather-related conditions.

faqs.question: Is daytime or evening better?
faqs.answer: Choose daytime for a clearer orientation to the riverbanks, or an evening departure if that atmosphere is your priority. Check actual daylight and departure times for your date.

guides.title: Budapest bars and nightlife: find your kind of evening
guides.description: Plan a Budapest evening around ruin bars, cocktail counters or a rooftop terrace, with a focused shortlist and official venue links.
guides.intro: An evening in Budapest does not need to become a long pub crawl. Choose the setting you want first: a courtyard to explore, a place to dance, a cocktail-focused bar or a rooftop table. The shortlist below introduces different formats so you can choose one or two stops that actually fit your plans.
highlights: Choose atmosphere before planning a route
Compare venue-specific table and terrace terms
Check the current programme and journey home

sections.title: Choose the kind of evening you want
paragraphs: Start by deciding whether you want conversation, live entertainment, dancing or a view. Our suggested approach is one main venue and an optional second stop nearby. Leave time for dinner and make a plan for the journey back to your accommodation.

A ruin-bar-style setting and a nightclub programme can overlap, but they are not the same experience. Look at the venue’s programme for your date rather than expecting every place to offer the same atmosphere at every hour.

sections.title: Ruin bars and a larger party complex
paragraphs: Szimpla Kert’s own information site provides its basic visitor details and concert programme. Begin there to check what is happening before choosing your visit. Treat it as a specific venue with its own schedule, rather than a generic promise about every ruin bar in the city.

Instant–Fogas describes a multi-space party complex on Akácfa Street, with different music settings under one roof. It is a candidate when dancing and a later evening are the priority. Check the current event details and entry conditions directly with the venue.

sections.title: A cocktail-focused alternative
paragraphs: Boutiq Bar presents a cocktail-led experience in central Budapest. It is a useful contrast to a multi-room party venue: review the current drinks offering and reservation options before deciding whether it fits your evening.

If conversation is the aim, ask about a suitable table rather than assuming every bar will be quiet. Menus, opening days and reservation conditions can change, so use the venue’s own information for the date you plan to go.

sections.title: Rooftop views: understand the table you are booking
paragraphs: High Note SkyBar is a rooftop venue beside the Basilica. Its official site distinguishes regular areas from separate panoramic-table and champagne-bar reservations with different minimum-consumption arrangements. Read the terms of the specific area you select.

For a view-led evening, ask about terrace availability and indoor alternatives before committing. A generic rooftop photograph does not guarantee a particular table or weather conditions. Leave room to change plans if an outdoor setting is the main attraction.

sections.title: Make the evening easy to enjoy
paragraphs: Check the venue’s latest programme, entry policy and reservation terms. Keep your chosen addresses saved, use the official transport information for the return and respect the residential streets around nightlife areas. Do not plan the next morning around an unrealistically early start.

This is an editorial introduction, not a paid ranking or a claim that we have personally visited the venues. We have linked the official sites so you can make the final choice from current information.

faqs.answer: No single rule applies. Check the individual venue and any table or terrace area you want, especially for a group.

guides.title: Downtown Pest walking guide: Parliament, Basilica and the Danube
guides.description: A relaxed self-guided walk through Budapest's central Pest sights, from Parliament to St Stephen's Basilica, Vörösmarty Square and the Chain Bridge.
guides.intro: Downtown Pest rewards wandering. Its central streets put architectural landmarks, historic cafés and the Danube within reach of one another. This self-guided route follows a loose north-to-south line through the city centre, leaving plenty of room for cafés, interior visits and unexpected detours. It is not a timed tour.
highlights: Start at Kossuth Square for the Parliament exterior
Continue to St Stephen's Basilica and Széchenyi István Square
Finish around Vörösmarty Square and the river, or extend to the Great Market Hall

sections.title: Start at Parliament and Kossuth Square
paragraphs: The Hungarian Parliament building is one of Budapest's defining riverfront landmarks. Start outside on Kossuth Lajos Square, where you can appreciate the building's scale without an interior ticket. If you want a guided visit inside, arrange the correct admission separately through the official visitor service.

A little farther along the embankment, Shoes on the Danube Bank commemorates people murdered on the riverbank during the Holocaust. Visit in a quiet, respectful spirit; it is not simply another photo stop.
bullets: Check Parliament entry and security rules before your date.
Keep the memorial visit unhurried and respectful.

sections.title: Find your way towards St Stephen's Basilica
paragraphs: Walk into the city-centre streets and make St Stephen's Basilica your next landmark. The surrounding square is inviting even if you choose not to enter. Religious services, visitor entry and any additional areas such as lookouts may follow separate rules.
Take a little time on the surrounding streets rather than treating the route as a direct dash between monuments. The city centre is as much about its façades and corner cafés as its headline sights.

sections.title: Head towards Chain Bridge and the river
paragraphs: From the basilica area, continue towards Széchenyi István Square and the Chain Bridge approaches. Gresham Palace is a useful architectural landmark on the square; the bridge opens the view towards the Buda hills and the Castle District opposite.
You can cross to Buda if your day has enough time, or stay on the Pest side to continue along the river. The view back across the Danube is one of the simplest pleasures of this route.

sections.title: Choose your café stop around Vörösmarty Square
paragraphs: Vörösmarty Square and nearby Váci Street make an easy final city-centre cluster. The streets are popular with visitors and shoppers; a short turn into the smaller surrounding lanes offers a change of pace.
Café Gerbeaud is a historic option on the square. Check its current menu and reservation rules on the official website if you plan to stop, rather than assuming a particular price or available table.

sections.title: Extend the walk towards the Great Market Hall
paragraphs: If you still have energy, continue south towards the Great Market Hall for a different atmosphere. This takes you beyond the compact core of District V, so allow extra time and check market trading hours.
For a shorter day, end at the river and enjoy the view. Many visitors get more from a shorter walk and an unplanned pause than from squeezing in one more distant sight.
bullets: This is a suggested walking sequence, not calculated live directions.
Check accessible transport options and venue entrances individually.
Plan around confirmed admissions, not guessed opening times.

faqs.question: Can I walk between the main Downtown Pest sights?
faqs.answer: Yes, the central landmarks in this guide lend themselves to a walking visit. Adapt the length to your pace and mobility needs.

faqs.question: Do I need to buy tickets for the whole route?
faqs.answer: No. The public streets and riverfront are open to explore without a tour ticket. Individual interiors and venues have separate admission arrangements.

faqs.question: Is the Jewish Quarter part of this walk?
faqs.answer: Not directly. The Jewish Quarter is mainly in nearby District VII; this route concentrates on the central Pest area, particularly District V.

guides.title: Budapest food and markets: first-time guide to cafés and local flavours
guides.description: Discover the Great Market Hall, famous Budapest cafés, classic Hungarian dishes and practical tips for a food-focused city break.
guides.intro: A good Budapest food day does not need a perfect checklist. Try a market, make time for a café and order a dish that interests you. This guide focuses on a small number of documented venues already in our directory, plus useful pointers for discovering Hungarian flavours at your own pace. It is not a restaurant ranking or a personal tasting review.
highlights: Go to the Great Market Hall to browse food stalls and ingredients
Consider Café Gerbeaud and New York Café for very different historic interiors
Check menu prices, allergens and reservations with each venue

sections.title: Start with the Great Market Hall
paragraphs: The Great Market Hall is an easy introduction to Budapest's market culture. Browse before buying and take time to compare stalls. Traditional ingredients, everyday produce and food-to-go can share the same building, but traders and selections change.

Market hours may differ from typical restaurant hours and can change around holidays. Verify the official opening information for your visit; avoid planning a final-day market stop around a guessed schedule.

sections.title: A café stop near Vörösmarty Square
paragraphs: Café Gerbeaud is a well-known historic café in central Pest. Its location makes it a convenient addition to a stroll around Vörösmarty Square and Váci Street.
The atmosphere may be a reason to visit as much as the menu. Check the current menu and booking arrangements directly, and decide whether the experience fits your budget and appetite.

sections.title: The theatrical interiors of New York Café
paragraphs: New York Café offers an ornate setting away from the compact District V core. It works best as a deliberate stop in a wider city walk rather than an assumed quick detour from the river.
Popular historic cafés may have waits or their own admission and reservation policies. Always verify the current arrangements with the venue instead of relying on old travel videos.

sections.title: What to look for on a Hungarian menu
paragraphs: Gulyás is a familiar starting point, alongside paprika-seasoned dishes, lángos and pastries such as rétes. These names describe broad traditions, not a promise that every café or stall will serve them in the same way.
If you have food allergies or other dietary requirements, ask the venue about the specific preparation and ingredients. Translations and menus can be incomplete.

sections.title: Leave room for your own discoveries
paragraphs: A market breakfast, riverside walk and afternoon coffee often make more sense than travelling across the city for three famous venues in one day. Choose stops close to where you already plan to be.
Treat this guide as an editorial starting point. GoToBudapest currently has three detailed food-and-market attraction entries, and those are not an exhaustive account of Budapest dining.

faqs.question: Is this a list of the best restaurants in Budapest?
faqs.answer: No. It is a curated introduction to markets and historic cafés, not a quality ranking or first-hand review of every venue.

faqs.question: Do I need a booking for a famous café?
faqs.answer: Reservation rules vary by venue and date. Use the official venue site for current details.

faqs.question: Can I rely on fixed food prices in travel guides?
faqs.answer: No. Check the venue's current menu and any service charges before ordering.

experiences.title: The Danube, at your pace
experiences.eyebrow: RIVERSIDE WALKS & A CITY SEEN FROM THE WATER
experiences.summary: Riverside walks, bridges and a city seen from the water.
experiences.description: How to experience Budapest along the Danube: riverside walks, bridges, viewpoints, green islands and cruise options, with the places to visit on both banks.
experiences.intro: The Danube is what holds Budapest together. Buda rises in hills on one bank and Pest spreads out flat on the other, and almost every classic view in the city is a view across the water. You can see the river from a bridge, a promenade, a hilltop terrace or a boat, and each gives you a different city.
highlights: Walk a stretch of either embankment before choosing a boat.
Check the exact departure pier and route for any cruise.
Evening departures vary with season and sunset.

faqs.question: Do I need a cruise ticket to enjoy the Danube?
faqs.answer: No. The public riverfront and bridges offer excellent views without booking a boat.

faqs.question: Are all cruises the same?
faqs.answer: No. Check the route, boarding pier, operating dates, inclusions and cancellation conditions for the specific departure.

sections.title: Walk both banks
paragraphs: Treat the riverfront as a route rather than a single stop. On the Pest side the embankment runs past the Chain Bridge, the Gresham Palace and the Hungarian Academy of Sciences towards the Parliament, and the Shoes on the Danube Bank memorial sits on the same stretch. On the Buda side the road below Castle Hill starts at Clark Ádám Square, the foot of the Chain Bridge and the funicular.
Each bank is the viewpoint for the other. The Pest promenade looks up at Castle Hill and the Bastion; the terraces on Castle Hill look back across to the Parliament and the Pest skyline.
bullets: Pest bank: Chain Bridge → Gresham Palace → Shoes on the Danube Bank → Parliament.
Buda bank: Clark Ádám Square → the foot of Castle Hill → the Castle Garden Bazaar.
Leave time to stop: most of the good moments here are unplanned.

sections.title: Cross the bridges on foot
paragraphs: The Chain Bridge is the obvious first crossing, linking Széchenyi István Square in Pest with Clark Ádám Square in Buda. Walking it rather than riding over gives you time to look downstream and upstream, and the bridge ends make natural starting points for either side of the city.
If you have time for a second crossing, pick one further along the river and compare the angle: every bridge frames the Parliament, Castle Hill and Gellért Hill a little differently.

sections.title: See the city from the water
paragraphs: A river cruise changes the scale of the city and puts the Parliament and Castle Hill in one frame. Formats differ widely: shorter daytime sightseeing trips, evening cruises when the riverside landmarks are lit, and longer trips with dinner or drinks.

GoToBudapest does not take bookings. Compare the route, departure pier, duration and what is included directly with each operator, and check accessibility for your own needs. Our guide explains how to choose between daytime, evening and dinner formats.

sections.title: Take a green break on the river
paragraphs: Two places let you leave the pavements without leaving the water. Margaret Island is a green island in the middle of the Danube for walks and a slower pace, and Kopaszi-gát is a waterside green area on the Buda side.

sections.title: Practical notes
paragraphs: Embankments are largely flat, but Castle Hill and Gellért Hill are steep, and surfaces can be uneven. Wind off the river can make evenings feel cooler than the forecast, so carry a layer outside summer. Opening times, boat departures and seasonal services change; confirm them with the operator before you travel.

experiences.title: Soak up the city
experiences.summary: Build a slower day around a thermal-bath visit.
experiences.description: A practical introduction to Budapest's thermal baths: how to choose between Széchenyi, Rudas, Lukács and other baths, which are seasonal, and which is closed for renovation.
experiences.intro: Bathing is part of how Budapest rests. Some baths are grand historic complexes, some are small Ottoman-era-style Turkish baths, and others are open-air pools that only run in season. The best visit is the one that suits the rest of your day, so choose the bath around the neighbourhood you are already exploring.
highlights: Pair Széchenyi with City Park.
Check Rudas session arrangements carefully.
Gellért Bath is closed for renovation.

faqs.question: Is Gellért Bath open?
faqs.answer: No. The operator reports a renovation closure with a planned reopening in 2028, which is not a confirmed date.

faqs.question: Are Budapest thermal baths suitable for children?
faqs.answer: Admission rules differ by venue and area. Check the operator's age restrictions before buying tickets.

sections.title: Pair a bath with a neighbourhood
paragraphs: Széchenyi Thermal Bath sits in City Park, so it fits naturally with a slow day around Heroes' Square and the park. On the Buda side, Rudas, Lukács and Veli Bej are close to the river and Gellért Hill, which makes them an easy follow-on to a morning on Castle Hill. Palatinus is on Margaret Island and works well after a walk on the island.
Thinking in neighbourhoods keeps travel time down and leaves the baths as the relaxed part of the day instead of an extra errand.

sections.title: Choose the kind of bath you want
paragraphs: Large thermal complexes combine several pools, steam and sauna areas. Turkish-style baths such as Rudas and Veli Bej offer a quieter, more traditional atmosphere, and both have sessions and access areas that vary by day and time, so check which one applies to your chosen date.
Open-air pools and beaches such as Palatinus, Lupa Beach and the Római Open-Air Bath are seasonal. Aquaworld Resort Budapest is a family-oriented water-park setting rather than a historic bath.

sections.title: Check the status before you plan
paragraphs: Gellért Thermal Bath is currently closed for renovation. The operator states that reopening is planned for 2028, which is not a confirmed date, so build your bath day around another venue. Seasonal baths can be closed outside their season and may change dates from year to year.

sections.title: Before you go
paragraphs: Bring swimwear and a towel unless the venue says it provides them, and check which facilities your ticket covers. Age rules, mixed or single-gender sessions, pool access and dress requirements differ between baths. GoToBudapest does not show ticket prices or availability, so confirm everything on the bath's own website.
bullets: Choose one bath rather than two: it is meant to be slow.
Check the day-specific session and access information.
Plan how you will get there and back before you get wet and tired.

experiences.title: A taste of Budapest
experiences.summary: Market mornings, cafés and Hungarian flavours.
experiences.description: Where to start with Hungarian food and drink in Budapest: the Great Market Hall, historic cafés, chocolate, Unicum and what to look for on a menu.
experiences.intro: Budapest is a city of long breakfasts and unhurried cafés. You do not need a list of restaurants to eat well here: start with a market, learn a few dishes, plan one grand café stop and let the rest of your wandering decide where you end up.
highlights: Browse the Great Market Hall with time to look around.
Pair Vörösmarty Square with a café stop.
Check menus, reservations and current hours directly.

faqs.question: Is this a list of the best restaurants in Budapest?
faqs.answer: No. It selects food-related places from the attraction directory and does not rank or review restaurants.

faqs.question: Should I book cafés?
faqs.answer: Check each café's current reservation policy and opening hours; they vary by venue.

sections.title: Start with the market
paragraphs: The Great Market Hall is a covered market hall for exploring food stalls and the atmosphere of a city market. Go earlier in the day for the best sense of how it works as a market, and treat it as a place to look, taste and ask questions as well as to buy.

sections.title: Plan one grand café stop
paragraphs: Budapest's historic cafés are destinations in their own right. The New York Café is known for its richly decorated interior, and Café Gerbeaud sits on Vörösmarty Square in the middle of downtown Pest. Both are popular, so allow for queues at busy times and check opening hours.
Pair a café stop with a walk: Vörösmarty Square and Váci Street are short walks apart, and Andrássy Avenue leads onwards from the centre.

sections.title: Sweet and spirited stops
paragraphs: For a food-flavoured museum visit, the Szamos Chocolate Museum is centred on the Szamos confectionery tradition, and House of Unicum tells the story of the Unicum brand and its production heritage. Check visit formats and age rules for the spirits-related venue directly.

sections.title: What to look for on a menu
paragraphs: Hungarian classics worth knowing by name include gulyás (a soup or stew), pörkölt (paprika-based stew), halászlé (fish soup), lángos (fried flatbread) and kürtőskalács (chimney cake). Cooking varies from place to place, so ask staff what they recommend.
bullets: Ask about ingredients and allergens directly; menus and recipes change.
Opening hours vary, and many places close on certain days.
GoToBudapest does not rate or recommend individual restaurants.

sections.title: Food history indoors
paragraphs: If the weather turns, the Hungarian Agricultural Museum in Vajdahunyad Castle and the Hungarian Museum of Trade and Tourism explore the country's agricultural, commercial and hospitality history.

neighbourhoods.title: The Castle District
neighbourhoods.description: A self-guided look at Buda's Castle District: how to get there, Matthias Church, Fisherman's Bastion, the palace area, quieter corners and practical notes on slopes and access.
neighbourhoods.intro: Castle Hill is Budapest's old Buda: cobbled lanes, courtyards, gateways and terraces above the Danube, with Matthias Church and Fisherman's Bastion at its heart. It rewards a slow half-day, and it is the best place to look back across the river at Pest.
highlights: Allow half a day for a relaxed first visit.
Fisherman's Bastion has separately ticketed upper areas.
Build in time for the backstreets and viewpoints beyond the main photo stop.

faqs.question: Is the Castle District free to visit?
faqs.answer: Walking the public streets is free. Museums, church interiors and the upper lookout at Fisherman's Bastion may require separate admission.

faqs.question: How much time should I allow?
faqs.answer: A half-day is a useful editorial allowance for the main viewpoints and quieter lanes. Add time for any museum or guided visit.

sections.title: Choose your way up
paragraphs: The funicular connects Clark Ádám Square, at the Buda end of the Chain Bridge, with the Castle area. You can also walk up, either by the stairs and paths from the river or through the Vienna Gate side, or take a bus: BKK lists routes 16, 16A and 116 for the upper Castle area, so check the current journey planner for your starting point. Whichever you choose, expect slopes.

sections.title: Begin at Trinity Square
paragraphs: Trinity Square is the centre of the district and sits beside Matthias Church. Take time to look at the details of the building, then continue to Fisherman's Bastion, whose terraces overlook the Danube and the Pest riverbank. The lower walkways and the upper lookout have different access arrangements, so check admission details for the level you want.

sections.title: Walk towards the palace
paragraphs: South of the church the hill opens into the Buda Castle palace complex. The Hungarian National Gallery and the Budapest History Museum are both inside it, and the Matthias Fountain and Savoyai Terrace are outside. Check museums and venues separately, because opening times and tickets are not shared.

sections.title: Find the quieter corners
paragraphs: Away from the main viewpoints the hill is calmer. The Tóth Árpád Promenade runs along the Castle wall, the Castle Garden Bazaar and the Tabán below the hill are green spaces, and the Medieval Jewish Prayer House introduces Buda's medieval Jewish heritage. The Hospital in the Rock is an underground museum beneath the hill.
bullets: Mary Magdalene Tower is currently listed as temporarily closed; check before planning an interior visit.
The Vienna Gate is a convenient entrance or exit on the northern side.

sections.title: Make it comfortable
paragraphs: Wear shoes with grip, because cobbles, steps and slopes are the norm. Leave time for the descent rather than rushing it, and confirm access arrangements for your own mobility needs before you go.

neighbourhoods.title: Downtown Pest
neighbourhoods.description: A walking guide to downtown Pest: the Parliament and riverfront, St. Stephen's Basilica, Andrássy Avenue, Vörösmarty Square, Jewish heritage sites and indoor museums.
neighbourhoods.intro: Pest is the flat, grand half of the city: wide boulevards, apartment blocks, cafés, concert halls and the Danube promenade. Most of the central sights are within walking distance of each other, which makes it ideal for a day without a fixed plan.
highlights: A mostly walkable city-centre area.
Combine St. Stephen's Basilica, the Chain Bridge and the riverside.
Váci Street and Vörösmarty Square bring cafés and shopping into the mix.

faqs.question: Is Downtown Pest the same as the Jewish Quarter?
faqs.answer: No. The historic city centre is primarily District V; the Jewish Quarter is mainly in neighbouring District VII and deserves a separate visit.

faqs.question: Can I see the main sights on foot?
faqs.answer: Many central sights are close enough for a walking day. Allow extra time for stops, accessibility needs and any booked interiors.

sections.title: Begin on the riverfront
paragraphs: Start by the Danube. The Hungarian Parliament stands on the Pest bank at Kossuth Square, and the promenade south of it passes the Shoes on the Danube Bank memorial, a riverside memorial to people murdered during the Holocaust, which deserves a respectful visit. Further on you reach the Chain Bridge, the Gresham Palace and the Hungarian Academy of Sciences around Széchenyi István Square.

sections.title: Basilica to Andrássy Avenue
paragraphs: St. Stephen's Basilica is a good starting point for the streets of the centre. From the area, Andrássy Avenue is the grand route out towards City Park, lined with the Hungarian State Opera, the Liszt Academy of Music and the House of Terror Museum and ending at Heroes' Square.
bullets: Opera and concert halls publish their own performance calendars and visitor programmes.
The House of Terror Museum addresses Hungary's experience of twentieth-century dictatorships; allow time and emotional space for it.

sections.title: Café, square and shopping street
paragraphs: Vörösmarty Square is a natural meeting point, home to Café Gerbeaud, and it connects to the pedestrian Váci Street. Pause for a coffee and cake before carrying on, or head for the New York Café for a more theatrical stop.

sections.title: Jewish heritage
paragraphs: The Dohány Street Synagogue is a significant synagogue and Jewish heritage site in central Pest. Check visiting arrangements, any dress requirements and security procedures with the site before you go, and treat it as a place of worship and memory.

sections.title: When it rains
paragraphs: Downtown has plenty of indoor options. The Hungarian National Museum traces the country's history, and the Great Market Hall makes an easy covered stop for food and atmosphere.
